conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: Which physiological states accentuate an innocent flow murmur?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Fever, anaemia and exercise
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Innocent flow murmurs are accentuated by increased/brisk flow - fever, anaemia, exercise and a thin chest wall. A murmur heard during a febrile illness may disappear on recovery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: A 10-day-old collapses in shock with grey, mottled skin, absent femoral pulses and a pink upper body but blue legs as the duct closes. What is the diagnosis and immediate treatment?
options: Critical (duct-dependent) coarctation of the aorta; prostaglandin E1 and resuscitation
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Critical (duct-dependent) coarctation of the aorta; prostaglandin E1 and resuscitation
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Neonatal collapse with absent femoral pulses and differential cyanosis (pink upper/blue lower body) as the duct closes indicates critical, duct-dependent coarctation. Treatment is prostaglandin E1 to reopen the duct plus resuscitation, then urgent surgical repair.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: An asymptomatic teenager is found to have hypertension in the arms, weaker/delayed femoral pulses, and a murmur heard over the back. What is the likely diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Coarctation of the aorta
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Upper-limb hypertension with radio-femoral delay/weak leg pulses and a murmur heard between the scapulae is classic coarctation of the aorta. Four-limb BP measurement (arm-leg gradient) is the key bedside test, and echocardiography is diagnostic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: Coarctation of the aorta is strongly associated with which chromosomal disorder and which valve anomaly?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Turner syndrome; bicuspid aortic valve
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Coarctation is strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) and a bicuspid aortic valve (present in up to two-thirds of infants with coarctation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: Which chest X-ray findings are characteristic of coarctation of the aorta?
options: Boot-shaped heart and egg on a string
The 'Figure 3 sign' and rib notching (rib notching usually only after ~age 5)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: The 'Figure 3 sign' and rib notching (rib notching usually only after ~age 5)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Coarctation classically shows the 'Figure 3 sign' (aortic contour) and rib notching from dilated collateral intercostal arteries eroding the ribs - rib notching usually appears only after about age 5, not in neonates.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: What is the single most useful bedside test for suspected coarctation of the aorta?
options: Four-limb blood pressure and pulse examination (arm-leg gradient, radio-femoral delay)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Four-limb blood pressure and pulse examination (arm-leg gradient, radio-femoral delay)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Four-limb blood pressure and pulse examination - demonstrating an arm-leg BP gradient and radio-femoral delay - is the key bedside test for coarctation. Echocardiography is the definitive diagnostic investigation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: After successful coarctation repair, which long-term complications require lifelong follow-up?
options: None - repair is curative with no follow-up
Re-coarctation, persistent/late hypertension, aneurysm and aortic dissection
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Re-coarctation, persistent/late hypertension, aneurysm and aortic dissection
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: Even after successful repair, coarctation needs lifelong follow-up for re-coarctation (especially after neonatal repair), persistent/late hypertension, aneurysm at the repair site, aortic dissection, and (with a bicuspid valve) aortic valve disease/endocarditis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.question: Why is critical neonatal coarctation described as 'duct-dependent' despite being an acyanotic lesion?
options: Because it causes a right-to-left shunt
Because the lower body is perfused via the PDA, so closure of the duct causes collapse and differential cyanosis
Because it always has an associated VSD
Because the duct supplies the coronary arteries
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.answer: Because the lower body is perfused via the PDA, so closure of the duct causes collapse and differential cyanosis
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Congenital Hear.explanation: In critical neonatal coarctation, blood reaches the lower body via the patent ductus arteriosus; when the duct closes, lower-body perfusion fails, causing shock and differential cyanosis - hence it is 'duct-dependent' and prostaglandin E1 is life-saving.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A boy with moderate learning disability and autistic features has a long face, large protruding ears and (after puberty) large testes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Learning disability with autism features, a long face, large protruding ears and post-pubertal macro-orchidism is classic Fragile X syndrome - the commonest inherited cause of learning disability and monogenic cause of autism.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What is the underlying genetic defect in Fragile X syndrome?
options: A CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, silencing it (full mutation >200 repeats)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: A CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, silencing it (full mutation >200 repeats)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Fragile X is caused by a CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in FMR1 on the X chromosome; a full mutation (>200 repeats) leads to hypermethylation and silencing of FMR1, with loss of FMRP. It shows anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Through which parent must a Fragile X premutation pass to expand to a full mutation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: A premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) expands to a full mutation only when transmitted through the MOTHER. Fragile X is X-linked, with males more severely affected and females variably affected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: An older man who is a Fragile X premutation carrier develops intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline. What is this?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Male premutation carriers over ~50 can develop FXTAS (tremor, cerebellar ataxia, cognitive decline/parkinsonism), often misdiagnosed as Parkinson's or essential tremor. Female carriers risk FXPOI (premature ovarian insufficiency).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A woman with unexplained premature ovarian insufficiency should be tested for which condition?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: About 20% of female Fragile X premutation carriers develop FXPOI (Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency), so FMR1 testing is indicated in unexplained premature ovarian insufficiency.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which test is definitive for Fragile X syndrome?
options: FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis (PCR + Southern blot for methylation)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis (PCR + Southern blot for methylation)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: The definitive test is FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis (PCR with Southern blot for methylation status), which quantifies the repeat number and methylation. It is indicated in unexplained developmental delay, autism, or a suggestive phenotype/family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A floppy neonate with a weak cry and poor feeding (failure to thrive) later develops an insatiable appetite and obesity, with short stature and hypogonadism. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: The evolving picture of neonatal hypotonia/poor feeding (failure to thrive) followed by childhood hyperphagia and obesity, with short stature and hypogonadism, is classic Prader-Willi syndrome (loss of paternally-expressed genes at 15q11-q13).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function of which genes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by loss of PATERNALLY-expressed genes at 15q11-q13 (usually paternal deletion, or maternal uniparental disomy). Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene at the same locus causes Angelman syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which disorder shares the same 15q11-q13 locus as Prader-Willi but results from loss of the MATERNAL copy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Angelman syndrome arises from loss of the maternal UBE3A gene at 15q11-q13 (the same locus as Prader-Willi). It causes severe learning disability, an ataxic 'puppet' gait, seizures and an inappropriately happy, laughing demeanour ('hAppy', mAternal).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What is the cornerstone of managing Prader-Willi syndrome to prevent its main cause of mortality?
options: Strict dietary control and a supervised eating environment
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Strict dietary control and a supervised eating environment
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: The cornerstone of Prader-Willi management is strict dietary control and a supervised, food-secure environment to prevent the life-threatening hyperphagia-driven obesity (and its complications - type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea), alongside growth hormone and sex hormone therapy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which is the first-line, definitive diagnostic test for Prader-Willi syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 is first-line and detects >99% of cases across all mechanisms, and importantly distinguishes Prader-Willi from Angelman syndrome. FISH/microarray and UPD studies then define the exact mechanism.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which therapy improves height, body composition and motor function in Prader-Willi syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Growth hormone therapy (started in early childhood) improves height, body composition and motor function in Prader-Willi syndrome, alongside strict dietary control and sex hormone replacement at puberty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A boy with short stature, a webbed neck, hypertelorism, ptosis and pulmonary valve stenosis has a NORMAL karyotype. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Short stature and a webbed neck with pulmonary stenosis in a boy with a NORMAL karyotype is Noonan syndrome (an autosomal dominant RASopathy, most often PTPN11). Turner syndrome affects only females and has a 45,X karyotype with left-sided lesions.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which cardiac lesion is most characteristic of Noonan syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Noonan syndrome characteristically causes right-sided lesions - pulmonary valve stenosis (commonest, ~50%) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy - in contrast to the left-sided lesions (bicuspid valve, coarctation) of Turner syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Noonan syndrome is caused by overactivation of which signalling pathway?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Noonan syndrome is a RASopathy caused by germline mutations activating the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway (commonest gene PTPN11, ~50%), which also underlies its increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Before surgery in a child with Noonan syndrome, which investigation is particularly important?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Noonan syndrome is associated with a bleeding tendency/coagulation defects, so a coagulation assessment is important before any surgery or dental work. Echocardiography (for pulmonary stenosis/HCM) is also essential.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: How is Noonan syndrome inherited, and what distinguishes it genetically from Turner syndrome?
options: Autosomal dominant with a NORMAL karyotype (Turner is 45,X)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Autosomal dominant with a NORMAL karyotype (Turner is 45,X)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Noonan syndrome is autosomal dominant (50% transmission; many cases de novo) with a NORMAL karyotype, affecting both sexes - unlike Turner syndrome (45,X, females only).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A child with a broad forehead, stellate irises, an overly friendly 'cocktail-party' personality and supravalvular aortic stenosis has which syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: An 'elfin' face with a stellate iris, a hypersocial 'cocktail-party' personality and supravalvular aortic stenosis is Williams syndrome (7q11.23 microdeletion including the elastin gene ELN).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which cardiovascular lesion is classic for Williams syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Supravalvular aortic stenosis (~75%) is the classic cardiovascular lesion in Williams syndrome, part of a progressive elastin arteriopathy (with peripheral pulmonary and renal artery stenoses and hypertension) requiring lifelong surveillance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which metabolic abnormality occurs in infancy in Williams syndrome, and what supplement should be avoided?
options: Transient hypercalcaemia; avoid vitamin D and calcium supplementation
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Transient hypercalcaemia; avoid vitamin D and calcium supplementation
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Williams syndrome causes transient infantile HYPERCALCAEMIA, so vitamin D and calcium supplementation should be AVOIDED (a low-calcium diet may be needed). Serum calcium should be monitored, especially in infancy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion of which gene/region?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Williams syndrome results from a 7q11.23 microdeletion including the elastin gene (ELN); elastin haploinsufficiency causes the characteristic arteriopathy (supravalvular aortic stenosis). It is usually de novo.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Why is anaesthesia potentially dangerous in Williams syndrome?
options: Risk of sudden death from coronary ostial stenosis and the progressive arteriopathy
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Risk of sudden death from coronary ostial stenosis and the progressive arteriopathy
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Williams syndrome carries a risk of sudden death (coronary ostial stenosis, arrhythmia) especially around anaesthesia, so cautious peri-operative management and lifelong cardiology follow-up are needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A microcephalic infant with hypertelorism and a round face has a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry and severe developmental delay. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: A high-pitched 'cat-like' cry with microcephaly and severe learning disability is the classic triad of Cri du Chat syndrome (deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, 5p-).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What is the underlying genetic abnormality in Cri du Chat syndrome?
options: Deletion of the short (p) arm of chromosome 5 (5p-)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Deletion of the short (p) arm of chromosome 5 (5p-)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Cri du Chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-), usually a de novo terminal deletion. It is the commonest deletion syndrome, and the deletion size determines severity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which is the confirmatory diagnostic test for Cri du Chat syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: A karyotype confirms Cri du Chat by visualising the 5p deletion; FISH or chromosomal microarray is used for doubtful or small deletions. Parental karyotyping is advised to exclude a balanced translocation carrier.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: In genetic counselling for Cri du Chat, why is parental karyotyping performed?
options: To confirm the diagnosis in the child
To exclude a balanced translocation carrier parent (which carries a higher recurrence risk)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: To exclude a balanced translocation carrier parent (which carries a higher recurrence risk)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Although most Cri du Chat cases are de novo (low recurrence), ~10-15% arise from an unbalanced parental translocation, so parental karyotyping is done to identify a balanced translocation carrier, who has a higher recurrence risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A newborn has a very small lower jaw, a tongue that falls backwards, and respiratory distress, with a U-shaped cleft palate. What is the diagnosis and immediate first-line airway management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Micrognathia, glossoptosis and airway obstruction (+ U-shaped cleft palate) is Pierre Robin sequence. First-line airway management is PRONE (or lateral) positioning, which lets the tongue fall forward and open the airway - many infants need nothing more.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Why is Pierre Robin described as a 'sequence'?
options: Because it occurs in a fixed sequence of patients
Because a single initiating defect (mandibular hypoplasia) triggers a cascade: tongue displacement -> cleft palate -> airway obstruction
Because it is inherited in sequence
Because the features appear in alphabetical order
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Because a single initiating defect (mandibular hypoplasia) triggers a cascade: tongue displacement -> cleft palate -> airway obstruction
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: A 'sequence' is a chain of malformations from a single initiating event. In Pierre Robin, the primary micrognathia forces the tongue up and back (glossoptosis), which blocks palatal shelf fusion (cleft palate) and obstructs the airway.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Which syndrome is the commonest association in syndromic Pierre Robin sequence, warranting ophthalmology assessment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: About half of Pierre Robin cases are syndromic, most commonly with Stickler syndrome (a collagen disorder causing myopia/retinal detachment, hearing loss and joint problems), so ophthalmology assessment is important; 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) is another association.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What is the main immediate danger of Pierre Robin sequence?
options: Life-threatening upper-airway obstruction from the backward-displaced tongue
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Life-threatening upper-airway obstruction from the backward-displaced tongue
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: The core danger is upper-airway obstruction from tongue-base (glossoptosis) obstruction, which can be life-threatening from the first hours of life - along with feeding difficulties, aspiration and failure to thrive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What tends to happen to the airway in Pierre Robin sequence as the child grows?
options: The jaw often 'catches up' with growth, improving the airway over time
It requires permanent tracheostomy in all cases
It has no relation to jaw growth
The cleft palate worsens the airway further
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: The jaw often 'catches up' with growth, improving the airway over time
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: The mandible often shows catch-up growth with age, improving the airway over time. Management is therefore often conservative (positioning, feeding support), with cleft palate repair around 6-12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: A tall adolescent boy has small firm testes, gynaecomastia, incomplete virilisation, a high FSH/LH and low testosterone. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Tall stature, small firm testes, gynaecomastia and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (low testosterone, high FSH/LH) in a male is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) - the commonest cause of male hypogonadism and infertility.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What is the definitive diagnostic test for Klinefelter syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: The karyotype (47,XXY) is definitive. The hormone profile shows low testosterone with high FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), and semen analysis typically shows azoospermia/oligospermia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: What is the mainstay of treatment in Klinefelter syndrome, and its key limitation?
options: Testosterone replacement, which does NOT restore fertility
hCG, which restores fertility in all
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Testosterone replacement, which does NOT restore fertility
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Testosterone replacement is the mainstay (virilisation, muscle/bone, libido, mood), but it does NOT restore fertility - and can suppress remaining spermatogenesis, so fertility (sperm retrieval/micro-TESE + ICSI) should ideally be discussed before starting testosterone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Compared with Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome differs in which key ways?
options: Klinefelter is male with an extra X and tall stature; Turner is female with a missing X and short stature (both have hypergonadotropic hypogonadism)
Klinefelter is short; Turner is tall
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.answer: Klinefelter is male with an extra X and tall stature; Turner is female with a missing X and short stature (both have hypergonadotropic hypogonadism)
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Both cause hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and infertility, but Klinefelter is male with an EXTRA X (47,XXY) and TALL stature, whereas Turner is female with a MISSING X (45,X) and SHORT stature.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.question: Men with Klinefelter syndrome have an increased risk of which malignancy relative to other men?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Genetic Syndrom.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome carries a markedly increased risk of breast cancer (related to gynaecomastia) compared with other men, along with increased risks of osteoporosis, VTE, metabolic syndrome/type 2 diabetes and mediastinal germ cell tumours.
